_about: What's new: one entry for each update, newest first. The first entry's version is the game's version. A minor entry is hidden until a player asks for every patch. Rules for every string: TONE.md.

items: While you prepare, the HUD shows what today's battle would take off your score if it began now, and how your last change moved it.

Teaching one student alone is far better than teaching a class: each student more adds a stroke, narrows the line and gives everyone less. A student holds two to four spells, and a new one replaces their weakest.
Interviews are one applicant at a time, and the college holds seven students.
Walls, pools and sub-towers hold their mana for as long as they stand, so building more leaves less for everything else. Lava Pool burns far less and holds far more.
Helpers take their mana again each time they finish, and go on until you send them away.
A battle lasts until every enemy has fallen or reached the tower, ten minutes at most.

The tower is laid out in two columns: the students' stations on the left, yours on the right, the invasion book between them, with paths worn across the floor. The field is smaller and the battle cameras closer.
Fewer words on each panel: how to use it is behind the ? by its title. A book you drag follows the pointer, and clicking an empty slot in the laboratory opens its tab.
The title screen is inside the tower: the camera turns slowly past every station while an archmage walks the room and the class waits on the benches.
Walking up to a station is easier to steer: the camera no longer turns to face it, so the keys always point the same way on the screen, and it comes down gently instead of dropping.
Every tile in the laboratory says what its piece does, with its numbers, and the spell's box reads the whole spell out in order.
Finding a book is a pile on the floor: drag each to its school's shelf, with no timer. Sort the pile with no mistake and you learn two books.

Send students to raid a rival from the invasion book. After a short run of jumps they join that rival's next battle, cast their own spells and attack the tower and its students. They are off your own towers while they are away.
Each student has a temperament, such as Hunter or Steadfast. Office hours draws how they decide as a tree, and in a battle you can watch it light up.
A student's health and speed grow with the spells they know: add up their effectiveness over every spell.
The tower is drawn like Ape Race's maps: faceted stone and timber, windows that let dusk light across the floor, full bookshelves, and each station dressed for what you do there.
Mages have arms and feet. They swing their arms as they walk, lift the staff to cast, hold a book up to read, and sit on the benches to listen.
Stand at a station and the camera comes down behind you, the way Ape Race follows its ape. Walk away and it rises again.
The battlefield has the same light: faceted grass, flowers and stones, and a haze far off.
The black outlines are gone, and the HUD is dark and see-through, so the scene shows behind it.
Office hours looks like its design: your class on the left, the student's stats and leanings in the middle, and a picture of the tower's seats on the right. Drag a student onto a seat, or click one.
Seat students at the map table too: open the map, choose Seat students, and drag a student's disc to another seat. Two students trade seats.
Sub-tower seats work: a student put on a sub-tower now stands on it.
The spell builder, the seal and the sorting game follow their designs: numbered sets, a tray with a tab for each kind, a dial with a ring for each piece, and shelves that fill as you sort.
Recruitment works: a key now counts once when you press it, however long you hold it. The star is the closing note, pressed with Space.
The spell laboratory is a builder: sets of an optional modifier, a payload and a trigger, left to right. A trigger opens the next set, and a Branch starts a second row from the first trigger.
Saving a spell seals it: turn each piece's ring until its glyph sits under the star. Sealing never changes the spell.
Office hours, a desk in the tower room: see each student's numbers and choose where they stand and what they cast, including a rotation of spells.
Effectiveness climbs steeply near a perfect drawing; only a flawless one reaches 100%.
Finding a book is a sorting game, and the pile holds books you already know. A librarian golem can search for you.
Lay walls a cell at a time by dragging; right-drag rubs out. Each cell rises in about a second.
Spells you cast on yourself with Q: Rising Tide, Deep Well and Quiet Mind.
Each student keeps at most four summons alive, for twelve seconds each.
An invasion goes to every rival at once.
Choose a difficulty in setup and on each trial. Normal is a little harder than before, and the preparation is 2:30.
Online: the host can copy a link to the room. Opening the link joins it.
A new title screen: a battle plays behind the menu while the camera circles it.
What's new: these notes, on the title screen. A New marker shows after an update.
Reading a book shows a large card for the piece it taught, with its glyph, what it does and its numbers, for three seconds or until the next book.
The glossary's spell pieces are the same cards.
Mana costs show with a mana symbol in the laboratory, on cards and in the glossary.
The map table's buttons answer every click while a wall rises.
Every archmage starts knowing Glass Wall and Raise Sub-tower. What you place costs its mana at once and rises a little later, while you do other things.
The map table: E opens the map, Esc closes it, and its panel sits beside the map.
The glossary: press G or the Glossary button at any time to read about every spell piece, your spells, every word and how to do each thing.
Each battle view has its own camera: drag to turn it, right-drag to move it, and turn the mouse wheel to zoom.
An invasion now starts with Invade and summons before any trigger, so every invasion you save sends something.
Buttons and chips are readable in a dark colour scheme.
Online play for up to four, by room code or by pasted codes, with computer rivals in the empty seats.
The first version: Versus against three computer rivals, a practice day, four trials with medals, and achievements.
